title: Repository onboarding
summary: Connect an existing code repository to ResearcherOS and build a research tree.
when: You have code but no research materials
what: Connects an existing experiment repository to ResearcherOS. The AI assistant reviews the code and related literature, leads a layered discussion (problem → program → causes and hypotheses → methods), checks that node titles make sense to an outside reader, writes the research files beside the code, and can place them on a separate branch so the code branch remains clean.
why: Avoid rebuilding a hypothesis tree manually when code already exists, while keeping research materials separate from code.
scenarios: A code repository has no research-materials directory yet
You want to formulate the problem and hypotheses using the code and literature
The team wants research materials on a separate branch
how: Open an AI-assistant chat in a workspace containing ResearcherOS and your repository. Ask it to connect the project path and follow this workflow through to completion, including a separate branch for research materials.
diagram: Environment checks and code review come first, followed by a literature check and four layers of conversation. Titles are then checked for clarity and style. Only after that are files written and, if needed, a separate branch created. An existing tree is never overwritten.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Check environment and review code] --> B[Review literature]
  B --> C[Discuss the problem]
  C --> D[Discuss the program]
  D --> E[Discuss causes and hypotheses]
  E --> F[Discuss methods]
  F --> G[Check title clarity]
  G --> H[Check writing style]
  H --> I[Write the research tree]
  I --> J[Create a separate repository branch]
example:
Connect /path/to/my_experiment to ResearcherOS.

Follow the onboarding workflow through to completion: build the hypothesis tree and save the research materials on a separate repository branch.

title: Git synchronization
summary: Pull and push research materials without committing secrets or platform code.
when: At session start and after experiments
what: Synchronizes only research materials: reports, the board, the hypothesis tree, and findings. It pulls repository changes first, then saves and pushes local edits when needed. Secrets and ResearcherOS platform code are excluded from commits.
why: Give the team one current view of the research so results do not remain local or overwrite other people's updates.
scenarios: Pull the latest materials at the beginning of a session
Share a completed experiment or new report
Handle the Sync button or an explicit synchronization request
how: Ask the AI assistant to synchronize a specific project, or click Sync in ResearcherOS. The workflow can use the deferred-push queue and local-changes status.
diagram: Every session starts with a pull, followed by a check for local changes. Changes are committed and pushed; otherwise the workflow waits and checks again later.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Session starts] --> B[Pull changes]
  B --> C{Local changes?}
  C -->|yes| D[Commit research materials]
  D --> E[Push to repository]
  C -->|no| F[Wait]
  F -->|after 30 minutes| B
example:
Synchronize project my-project with its repository:
pull changes first, then push local research-material edits if there are any.

title: Experiment design
summary: Turn an experiment idea into a clear plan, one question at a time, before any run.
when: A new card or experiment specification
what: This is planning, not execution. The AI assistant interviews you with one question and a recommended answer per turn. It covers the claim, metric and verdict rule, boundaries, implementation, tables and charts, subtasks, and definition of done. The result is a draft specification in the report and a backlog card.
why: Prevent experiments from starting with a vague hypothesis or ambiguous success criterion.
scenarios: You have a broad idea but need an experiment card
The specification lacks a metric, subtasks, or a verdict threshold
You need to record decisions one question at a time
how: Ask the AI assistant to design or grill an experiment for a specific method, one question per turn. Use the separate card-execution workflow for the run itself.
diagram: Topics follow their dependencies: context and claim, metrics and boundaries, implementation and visualizations, then subtasks and a backlog card. A branch is skipped only when you explicitly say it is unnecessary.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Project context] --> B[Claim and motivation]
  B --> C[Metric and verdict rule]
  C --> D[Boundaries and dependencies]
  D --> E[Data, model, launch command]
  E --> F[Tables and charts]
  F --> G[Subtasks and definition of done]
  G --> H[Backlog card]
  H --> I[Draft report specification]
example:
Design a new experiment for method <method>:
grill the specification one question at a time and recommend an answer at every step.

title: Card execution
summary: Have the AI assistant run a card's experiment from in progress to report, finding, and done.
when: Execute the card or run an experiment
what: The assistant owns the card end to end: moves it to in progress, performs the experiment described by report subtasks (code, runs, metrics, and artifacts), checks off work, records results, reviews the report, moves the card to done, formulates a finding, and synchronizes when needed. It can maintain a live-progress note. Use autoresearch for multi-hour runs with separate roles.
why: Make card execution mean a complete experiment while keeping the board, report, and facts aligned.
scenarios: A request requires a real run rather than advice
A short experiment the assistant can run and measure
A long remote run where autoresearch adds roles
An in-progress card still needs its subtasks and report completed
how: Name the project and card, and ask for complete execution: in progress, every experiment subtask, done, and a recorded finding. Ask for autoresearch when a long run needs roles.
diagram: Moving to in progress is followed by actual subtask execution, results, report review, done status, a finding, and synchronization. Autoresearch roles fit inside the execution step.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Find card] --> B[Move to in progress]
  B --> C[Read specification and subtasks]
  C --> D[Run experiment subtasks]
  D --> E[Check off completed work]
  E --> F[Record results]
  F --> G[Review report]
  G --> H[Move to done]
  H --> I[Formulate finding]
  I --> J[Synchronize]
example:
Execute card <title or id> in project <project> end to end:
move it to in progress, run every experiment subtask, update progress, and finish with done status and a finding.

title: Card autoresearch
summary: Run one card over a long period with Manager, Researcher, and Debugger roles.
when: Systematic research or a multi-hour run
what: The Manager moves the card to in progress and configures the live window and state file. The Researcher starts and monitors the job and checks off subtasks. The Debugger only diagnoses failures and records recommendations; code changes and restarts remain the Researcher's responsibility. Kanban, reporting, and done status follow card execution.
why: Keep multi-hour or remote runs from becoming start-and-forget jobs by separating operation, monitoring, and diagnosis.
scenarios: A request for systematic research or autoresearch
A job lasting hours or days that needs monitoring and failure triage
A project launch skill needs a shared role protocol
how: Ask for autoresearch and provide the project plus card ID or title. Mention any project-specific launch skill. Roles and cadence come from this workflow; kanban handling comes from card execution.
diagram: The Manager acts once at the beginning. Researcher and Debugger then operate in parallel: the Researcher checks job health frequently, while the Debugger performs scheduled and incident triage. The workflow ends with a report and done status.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  U[User request] --> M[Manager: in progress + live view + state]
  M --> R[Researcher: start job]
  R --> W[Watch: every minute × 20, then every 20 min]
  R --> D[Debugger: every 10 min]
  W -->|failure| I[Call debugger]
  I --> D
  D -->|recommendation in state| W
  W -->|complete| F[Report + done + finding]
example:
Run systematic research for card <id> in project <project>:
use Manager → Researcher → Debugger roles and monitor progress throughout.

title: Finding from a completed card
summary: Turn a completed experiment into a plain-language question and answer stored in the findings database.
when: A card reaches the done column
what: Reads the method context, card, and report, then writes a research question and answer understandable without project jargon. Technical figures are separated. It labels the finding as definite or tentative, records its importance, and saves it in the project's answer database.
why: Leave a concise, reusable answer after every experiment, not just a report.
scenarios: A completed card has no structured finding
A result must be explained without internal jargon
The knowledge base needs certainty and importance metadata
how: Ask the assistant to process a completed card and save its research finding. Provide the project and card ID or title.
diagram: Gather the method, card, and report; formulate a clear question and answer; separate technical detail; assign certainty and importance; save the result.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Completed card] --> B[Read method and report]
  B --> C[Write plain-language question]
  C --> D[Write answer and technical details]
  D --> E[Set certainty and importance]
  E --> F[Save finding]
example:
Process completed card <id> in project <project>:
formulate a clear research question and answer, then save the finding.

title: Experiment report review
summary: Check a report for evidence, reproducibility, and valid knowledge-base integration.
when: Before a report is accepted or published
what: Reviews a working report against its specification, metrics, decision rule, artifacts, caveats, and proposed insights. It distinguishes measured facts from interpretation, checks reproducibility, and validates IDs and structured findings.
why: Prevent unsupported verdicts, irreproducible results, and malformed insights from entering the knowledge base.
scenarios: A run report is ready for ingestion
A card is about to move to done
A working report needs conversion into a public report
how: Ask the assistant to review a specific report and include the project plus report or card path.
diagram: Check links and specification, execution evidence, metrics and verdict rule, caveats, and insights. Return corrections or approve ingestion and publication.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Open report and specification] --> B[Check links and reproducibility]
  B --> C[Verify metrics and artifacts]
  C --> D[Apply decision rule]
  D --> E[Review caveats]
  E --> F[Validate structured insights]
  F --> G{Ready?}
  G -->|no| H[Request corrections]
  G -->|yes| I[Ingest or publish]
example:
Review the report for card <id> in project <project>:
check evidence, reproducibility, the verdict rule, caveats, and the integration block.

title: Research prose style
summary: Edit research text into clear prose without filler or invented claims.
when: Writing or polishing reports, documentation, and papers
what: Improves structure, clarity, terminology, and sentence rhythm while preserving technical meaning and evidence boundaries. It removes generic filler, repetition, fake quotations, and unsupported certainty.
why: Make research writing readable and credible without changing what the experiment established.
scenarios: A correct report is hard to read
A public document contains repetitive or AI-like phrasing
Terminology and claims need consistency
how: Ask the assistant to edit a document with this workflow while preserving facts, citations, uncertainty, and terminology.
diagram: Identify audience and claims, check terminology and evidence boundaries, rewrite for clarity, remove filler, and verify meaning preservation.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Read audience and purpose] --> B[Map claims and evidence]
  B --> C[Normalize terminology]
  C --> D[Rewrite for clarity]
  D --> E[Remove filler and repetition]
  E --> F[Verify meaning is preserved]
example:
Edit this report with the research-prose workflow:
make it clear and concise while preserving every fact, citation, and uncertainty boundary.

title: Knowledge curation
summary: Maintain a coherent knowledge base from verdicts, findings, reports, and curated documents.
when: After new findings or when the knowledge base needs cleanup
what: Audits project knowledge, links findings to methods and reports, removes duplication, preserves provenance, and keeps curated documents distinct from generated indexes. It highlights contradictions and stale conclusions rather than silently choosing one.
why: Keep accumulated research usable as the project grows and prevent summaries from drifting from source reports.
scenarios: Experiments produced overlapping findings
The dashboard contains stale or duplicated material
A curated overview needs links to evidence
how: Ask the assistant to curate a project knowledge base. It should inspect reports and generated indexes, then edit only appropriate curated sources.
diagram: Inventory sources, check provenance and duplicates, identify contradictions, update curated documents, and regenerate indexes through normal hooks.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Inventory verdicts and findings] --> B[Trace each item to a report]
  B --> C[Find duplicates and contradictions]
  C --> D[Update curated documents]
  D --> E[Regenerate indexes]
  E --> F[Review knowledge dashboard]
example:
Curate the knowledge base for project <project>:
check provenance, duplicates, contradictions, and update the appropriate curated documents.

title: Related Work queue
summary: Process a literature task from the UI queue and save the review on the Related Work page.
when: A Related Work task appears in the queue
what: Accepts a literature task, retrieves its project and cluster context, writes the review, and saves the answer back to the Related Work page.
why: Let literature analysis begin from UI-selected clusters and appear on the page without manual copying.
scenarios: A Related Work task entered the queue
A Literature Inbox received a signal
An accepted answer needs completion or resaving
how: Ask the assistant to process the queue in order: accept → retrieve context → write review → save answer.
diagram: Every queue step is required: acceptance changes the UI state, and saving returns the text from the assistant to the page.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[UI queue] --> B[Accept task]
  B --> C[Retrieve context]
  C --> D[Write review]
  D --> E[Save answer to page]
example:
Check the Related Work queue and process its task:
accept → retrieve context → write the review → save the answer.

title: Paper to PDF
summary: Build a project paper draft from the queue and place its PDF in the repository.
what: Accepts a paper task, collects context from the project tree and reports, writes a draft, builds a PDF in the repository, and closes the task so the interface updates.
why: Turn an accumulated research graph into a paper draft without manually collecting material from many directories.
scenarios: Generate paper was clicked
The paper queue contains a task
A Paper Inbox received a new-paper signal
how: Ask the assistant to check the paper queue and process a task through PDF creation and closure.
diagram: Acceptance lets the interface show work in progress; closure after the PDF is built prevents the task from remaining pending.
mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Paper queue] --> B[Accept task]
  B --> C[Collect project context]
  C --> D[Draft paper]
  D --> E[Build PDF in project]
  E --> F[Close task]
example:
Check the paper queue and process its task:
accept → collect context → draft → PDF → close.

title: Chat from the interface
summary: Answer a panel question using findings first and reports when needed.
when: A question arrives from the Ask agent panel
what: Retrieves a question from the UI queue. If it matches an existing finding, it answers quickly. Otherwise it reads the necessary reports and returns an answer to the chat panel. Operation can use a persistent Inbox chat, editor hooks, or an API key.
why: Answer project questions from accumulated findings and reports while preserving research context.
scenarios: A new question appears in Ask agent
The queue has unanswered questions at session start
An answer must rely on stored findings
how: Ask the assistant to check the interface-question queue and answer pending items. Configure an Inbox chat or hooks for faster operation.
diagram: Check the findings database first; read reports only when no suitable finding exists. Always return the answer to the queue for display.
mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Question from interface] --> B{Matching finding?}
  B -->|yes| C[Quick answer]
  B -->|no| D[Read reports]
  D --> E[Return answer to queue]
  E --> F[Show in chat panel]
example: Check the interface-question queue and answer all pending items using the ResearcherOS chat workflow.
